title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yezeyuan Zheng, Ziyang Hu, Maojun Sun. Ruijian Han, Jian Huang, Guanhua Chen, Jie Liu
abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Surrogate-guided reinforcement learning enriched virtual perovskite recipe shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors, without establishing fabricated-device performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help prioritize perovskite compositions, device layers, and processing recipes before costly fabrication.
method: Generate device recipes using reinforcement-learning policies guided by a frozen TabPFN surrogate.
Assess neighborhood support against 890 experimentally measured devices.
Compare three learned policies with six baselines using 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run.
infographic.evidence_signal: At top-100 selection, PPO and recurrent PPO achieved neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23% and 24%, versus 2.9% for Pure Random and 10% for the strongest baselines on this metric.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental performance, seed robustness, and matched-budget advantage remain unproven; composition-family support also drops sharply at stricter similarity thresholds.
infographic.paper_title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
authors: YanKai Chen, Zhi Wan, ZiHao Li, Tao Jing
abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

infographic.key_insight: Training language models on structured experimental evidence enabled stronger perovskite reasoning and guided a contact-material choice that outperformed the expert-preferred alternative.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evidence-grounded AI can help prioritize perovskite device experiments, with the selected contact yielding 27.05% efficiency and 96.74% retention after 1,000 hours of dark thermal ageing at 85°C.
method: Reconstruct expert-calibrated evidence records from 4,035 training articles.
Adapt OpenPerov using links among experimental strategies, controls, observations and mechanisms.
Refine selected responses with retrieved evidence and experimentally test a K-based self-assembled monolayer analogue.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 800-question PSM-Bench, OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems; retrieval-assisted OpenPerov Pro increased Scientific Mastery from 87.6 to 89.1.
infographic.watch_item: Dark thermal ageing and one demonstrated contact-selection task do not establish operational stability or generalization across device architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization

title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors
authors: Zixu Huang, Julisa Juarez, Akash Dasgupta, David S. Ginger
abstract: Buried interfaces play a critical role in the operational stability of perovskite optoelectronic devices, yet remain challenging to probe non-destructively. Here, we demonstrate a multiwavelength photoluminescence-based approach exploiting the wavelength-dependent absorption of perovskites, enabling fast, and non-destructive probing of depth-sensitive degradation behavior of perovskite devices under operational conditions. Using ultraviolet (UV) light-soaking with different indium tin oxide (ITO) modifiers as a test case, we employ wide-field photoluminescence (PL) imaging, time-resolved photoluminescence (trPL) and ideality factor measurements with different wavelength excitation to characterize degradation behavior of both perovskite thin films and photovoltaic devices under UV soaking. Using only nondestructive characterization, we show that UV-induced degradation in p-i-n perovskite solar cells occurs preferentially at the HTL interface, adversely affecting device stability, consistent with ex-situ destructive tests. Our results also show that modifying the buried interface with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane reduces UV-induced damage at the buried interface, thus improving the UV stability of both perovskite films and devices. This work establishes a fast, non-destructive strategy to screen depth-dependent degradation in perovskite devices, offering insights for interface design and stability optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Multiwavelength photoluminescence non-destructively reveals depth-dependent UV damage in perovskite solar cells, with degradation concentrated near the buried hole-transport-layer interface.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Depth-sensitive optical screening can guide interface design, including 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane modification to improve UV stability.
method: Use wavelength-dependent absorption to probe different depths.
Combine wide-field PL imaging, time-resolved PL and ideality-factor measurements during UV soaking.
Compare perovskite films and p-i-n devices with different ITO interface modifiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nondestructive measurements localized UV degradation near the HTL interface, consistent with destructive tests, and showed reduced damage with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane modification.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative stability gains or depth resolution, and UV-soaking results alone do not establish long-term operational durability.
infographic.paper_title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors

title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells
authors: Jiaxin Wu, Hongzhuo Wu, Zuhong Zhang, Xiaoyu Guan, Jinbo Zhao, Yuting Guo
abstract: Although inverted perovskite solar cells now deliver certified efficiencies approaching their single-junction limits, their practical deployment remains constrained by the thermo-mechanical fragility of buried interfaces under realistic temperature fluctuations. Here, we identify thermo-mechanically driven, stress-accumulation-dominated adhesion failure at self-assembled monolayer-based buried interfaces as a critical failure mode in inverted perovskite solar cells. To address this issue, we propose an interfacial robustness design strategy based on a homometallic halide pretreatment, which constructs a chemically compatible and highly anchorable interfacial environment on transparent conductive oxides to guide the ordered assembly of SAMs. This interfacial treatment increases the density of surface hydroxyl species and enables hierarchical multipoint interfacial anchoring dominated by metal-oxygen coordination, with Cl- induced hydrogen-bonding interactions acting cooperatively, thereby enhancing anchoring robustness and improving tolerance to thermo-mechanical stress accumulation. With this interfacial strategy, the devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 27.3% (26.9% certified) and retain 94% of their initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between -40 and 85 degrees C (ISOS-T-3). These results demonstrate that rational regulation of buried interfacial anchoring architectures can simultaneously enhance device efficiency and long-term operational reliability, offering a viable pathway toward high-efficiency and durable perovskite photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical multipoint anchoring strengthens buried interfaces in inverted perovskite solar cells, improving efficiency and resistance to thermal cycling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering adhesion at self-assembled monolayer interfaces offers a route to reduce thermo-mechanical failure in high-efficiency perovskite photovoltaics.
method: Pretreat transparent conductive oxides with a homometallic halide to guide ordered self-assembled monolayer formation.
Increase surface hydroxyl density to strengthen metal–oxygen coordination.
Add cooperative chloride-induced hydrogen bonding for robust multipoint anchoring.
infographic.evidence_signal: Devices achieved 27.3% efficiency (26.9% certified) and retained 94% of initial efficiency after 400 temperature cycles between −40 and 85 °C under ISOS-T-3.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish large-area manufacturing compatibility or durability under combined outdoor stresses.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical interfacial anchoring for durable perovskite solar cells

title: Dynamic Molecular Transformation Mediated Crystallization Regulation and Interface Passivation in Tin Based Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Ying Tang, Zuhong Zhang, Hongzhuo Wu, Zhihao Li, Zhenhuang Su, Yonggang Yang
abstract: Tin-based perovskites are promising candidates for lead-free photovoltaics but suffer from labile Sn$^{2+}$ coordination, rapid crystallization, and severe interfacial defects. Here, we develop a dynamic molecular transformation using 1-acetylpiperazine (PX) to regulate crystallization and interface chemistry simultaneously. During nucleation and growth, the carbonyl group coordinates with Sn$^{2+}$ to stabilize precursor complexes, moderate supersaturation, and enable controlled crystal growth. Upon annealing, PX undergoes in situ molecular transformation, suggested to form amidinium-functionalized species that preferentially occupy surface A-site vacancies, forming a passivation layer and suppressing nonradiative recombination. This coupled bulk-to-interface evolution yields compact, highly crystalline films with improved optoelectronic quality. Devices achieve a power conversion efficiency of 15.18% and retain 94.1% of initial efficiency after 500 h of continuous illumination. This work demonstrates a dynamic molecular engineering approach integrating crystallization control and interface passivation, providing a pathway toward efficient and stable lead-free perovskite photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: 1-acetylpiperazine (PX) dynamically couples crystallization control with interface passivation to improve lead-free tin-based perovskite solar cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single additive addresses both film formation and interfacial defects, offering a route toward more efficient and stable tin-based photovoltaics.
method: PX carbonyl groups coordinate with Sn²⁺ to stabilize precursor complexes and moderate supersaturation.
Controlled crystal growth produces compact, highly crystalline films.

infographic.watch_item: The proposed annealing-induced molecular transformation requires further confirmation; the abstract does not specify device statistics or illumination-test conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Molecular Transformation Mediated Crystallization Regulation and Interface Passivation in Tin Based Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Controlling Surface Chemistry in Tin-Lead Perovskites for High-Efficiency Solar Cells
authors: Lijun Chen, Sitong Zhao, Gaukhar Nigmetova, David Garcia Romero, Matteo Pitaro, Sofia Lerda
abstract: Interfacial nonradiative recombination limits tin-lead perovskite photovoltaics. Here we show that neutral ethylenediamine chelates undercoordinated metals at tin-rich surfaces, weakens metal-iodide bonds, and removes excess tin, reconstructing the surface towards a stoichiometric tin-to-lead ratio. In contrast, protonated ethylenediammonium iodide initially passivates undercoordinated metal sites before undergoing defect-assisted deprotonation. Atomistic simulations reveal that subsurface iodide vacancies promote iodide migration and lower the energetic cost of deprotonation. Ethylenediamine-induced reconstruction produces stronger n-type surface character, facilitates electron extraction into C60, and suppresses interfacial nonradiative recombination, enabling methylammonium-free solar cells with a power conversion efficiency of 25.86%. Together, these distinct surface reaction pathways and the defect-assisted evolution of the passivating species underscore the importance of understanding perovskite surface chemistry for the rational design of molecular passivation strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Ethylenediamine reconstructs tin-rich tin–lead perovskite surfaces toward stoichiometric composition, improving electron extraction and suppressing interfacial nonradiative recombination.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling molecular protonation and surface defects offers a route to more efficient methylammonium-free perovskite solar cells.
method: Compare neutral ethylenediamine with protonated ethylenediammonium iodide surface treatments.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 25.86% power conversion efficiency and simulations showing that subsurface iodide vacancies lower the energetic cost of deprotonation.
infographic.watch_item: Long-term stability and manufacturing-scale reproducibility of the reconstructed surfaces are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling Surface Chemistry in Tin-Lead Perovskites for High-Efficiency Solar Cells

title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements
authors: Nabanita Sarker, Hafiz Imtiaz
abstract: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning can diagnose degradation mechanisms in simulated lead-free solar cells, but strong predictions require representative training data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Replacing Spiro-OMeTAD with CuI raises simulated efficiency from 19.6% to 21.6%, almost entirely through improved fill factor.
method: Generate approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations of RbSn₀.₅Ge₀.₅I₃ solar cells.
Compare surrogate models trained on factorial-grid and Latin hypercube samples.

infographic.paper_title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements

title: Amorphous selenium-alloyed TeOx thin-film solar cells
authors: Zhaoheng Ling, Linqu Luo, Chrysa Aivalioti, Temur Maksudov, Mengxi Zhang, Theodoulos Kalogerakis
abstract: Tellurium dioxide (TeO$_2$) is a wide-bandgap oxide with attractive processing versatility and emerging p-type semiconducting behaviour, making it a promising material system for optoelectronic and photovoltaic applications. However, TeO$_2$-derived thin films prepared by scalable manufacturing processes, such as vacuum sublimation, can contain residual metallic Te$^0$ species that introduce trap states, limit hole transport, and promote carrier recombination. Here, we demonstrate a selenium alloying strategy to control the defect chemistry of vacuum-sublimed TeO$_x$ films. TeO$_2$:Se powder mixtures (90:10~wt\%) were thermally evaporated and subsequently annealed in air at 225~$^\circ$C for up to 9~h, yielding amorphous TeO$_x$:Se films with an optical bandgap of 0.98~eV under optimised conditions. Structural, chemical, optical, and electrical analyses show that prolonged annealing promotes Se redistribution, suppresses residual Te$^0$ to approximately 0.4\%, reduces the film's surface roughness, and shifts the valence-band edge. To evaluate the potential of TeO$_x$:Se for photovoltaic applications, we fabricated thin-film solar cells with an ITO/ZnO/TeO$_x$:Se/MoO$_x$/Ag architecture. Devices based on an 80~nm TeO$_x$:Se active layer annealed for 9~h exhibit optimal performance, with broadband photocurrent generation from 300 to 1000~nm, yielding an open-circuit voltage of 0.50~V, a short-circuit current density of 8.50~mA~cm$^{-2}$, a fill factor of 0.44, and a maximum power conversion efficiency of approximately 1.87\%. These results establish selenium-alloyed TeO$_x$ as a viable oxide-derived absorber for thin-film photovoltaics and highlight chemical-state control as an effective route for improving photovoltaic performance.

infographic.key_insight: Selenium alloying and air annealing suppress residual metallic tellurium in amorphous TeOx films, enabling thin-film solar cells with approximately 1.87% efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Chemical-state control offers a route to improve oxide-derived photovoltaic absorbers fabricated by scalable vacuum deposition.
method: Thermally evaporate a 90:10 wt% TeO₂:Se powder mixture.

infographic.watch_item: The 9-hour annealing step may constrain manufacturing throughput, while long-term stability and large-area reproducibility are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Amorphous selenium-alloyed TeOx thin-film solar cells

title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
authors: A. Benedit-Cardenas, G. Masset, M. Bugnet, M. Martirosyan, G. Steciuk, S. Migot
abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: Atomically engineered LaVO3/PrVO3 superlattices enable composition-dependent tuning of antiferromagnetic ordering alongside controlled structural distortions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Layer-by-layer oxide growth offers a route to tailoring magnetic properties through strain and interface design; the abstract does not report AI methods or solar-cell applications.
method: Grow LaVO3/PrVO3 superlattices by molecular beam epitaxy on (001) SrTiO3.

infographic.watch_item: Trilinear structural coupling is inferred indirectly from displacement and hybridization proxies, and the abstract provides no quantitative tuning range.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices

title: Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource
authors: Mark G. Raizen, Aaron Barr, Ahmed Helal
abstract: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed photonic Maxwell’s demon uses wavelength-selective mirrors and irreversible wavelength conversion to admit sunlight while trapping converted radiation for energy use.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The concept could improve solar-thermal storage and thermophotovoltaic conversion through repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization in the ideal limit.
method: Pair a multilayer dielectric mirror with a material that irreversibly converts transmitted photons to longer wavelengths.
Construct a 3D enclosure that admits visible light and reflects converted infrared radiation inward.
Combine the enclosure with a blackbody absorber and, for thermophotovoltaics, an ultra-low-bandgap photovoltaic cell.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical proposal and analysis, citing the 93.3% Landsberg limit as an ideal thermodynamic target rather than a demonstrated efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: Real performance depends on nonideal spectral selectivity, conversion losses, and heat leakage; no experimental validation or AI method is reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource

title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
authors: Marcos Soldera, Robert Baumann, Bogdan Voisiat, Wilhelm Pfleging, Penghui Zhu, Jörn Bonse
abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.

infographic.key_insight: This review chapter surveys laser processing across fusion, solar energy, electrochemical systems, and batteries; it is not specifically an AI solar-cell study.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Laser techniques offer routes to optimize photovoltaic cells, recycle solar modules, and improve battery manufacturing and electrochemical performance.
method: Review laser-driven fusion facilities and key laser parameters.
Survey photovoltaic optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted module recycling.
Examine multiscale surface texturing and laser processing for lithium-ion batteries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a broad technology review but reports no quantitative results, datasets, or comparative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Industrial scalability and performance benefits require application-specific validation beyond the overview provided in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications

title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
authors: Arash Omidi, Tanmay Mishra, Mads R. Almassalkhi
abstract: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.

infographic.key_insight: Constraint-aware reinforcement learning reduces battery sizing needs for PV ramp-rate smoothing while maintaining grid-code compliance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Joint controller design and battery sizing can reduce required storage power and energy capacity for grid-connected PV systems.
method: Learn a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without deployment-time forecasts.
Constrain actions using a feasibility interval incorporating ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge limits.
Benchmark against full-horizon, noncausal optimization using an input-convex neural network.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three real-world PV datasets at a 10%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduced peak battery power by 8.7–10.4% and energy capacity by 47.5–62.6% versus conventional ramp-rate control.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the evaluated datasets and robustness to deployment conditions require validation; this study concerns PV system control, not perovskite cell materials.
infographic.paper_title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller

title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
authors: Guibin Chen, Emma Fan, Yuzhang Lin
abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.

infographic.key_insight: Segmentation-guided direct regression estimates rooftop PV capacity more accurately than forcing predictions to equal mask-derived area times power density.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Aerial-image capacity estimates could help distribution planners fill gaps in installation-level PV inventories when interconnection records are incomplete.
method: Retain U-Net segmentation to identify PV regions.
Use soft-mask pooling to extract PV-region features and area descriptors.
Directly regress nonnegative capacity rather than an area–density product.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations, Direct Head reduced MAE by 8.7% and 12.5% and symmetric MAPE by 14.0% and 20.7% versus a parameter-matched area-density neural model under the original split and department-based holdout, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond French rooftop installations and across different aerial-imagery conditions remains unestablished by the reported evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery

title: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures
authors: Ajeet Singh, Sudhir Kumar Saini, Hriday Kumar Pal, Cara Elisabeth Bradsher, Sirous Khabbaz Abkenar, Roman Krahne
abstract: Engineering internal interfaces within single crystals remains challenging, particularly in soft ionic materials such as layered halide perovskites (LHPs), for which conventional lithographic approaches are difficult to implement. Here we report a solvent/antisolvent-driven strategy for controlled etching of LHP microcrystals, producing well-defined rectangular cavities. Etching initiates at the top surface and proceeds preferentially along the crystallographic [100] and [010] directions. Cavity dimensions are tuned through etching time, temperature and etchant composition. The reaction can be interrupted and resumed, enabling stepwise cavity evolution through successive etching cycles. The resulting cavities serve as confined templates for regrowth of compositionally distinct LHPs, yielding endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal architectures. The approach extends across diverse LHP compositions and antisolvent systems, while sequential precursor addition controls the extent of internal regrowth. This strategy establishes a route to engineering internal heterointerfaces in single-crystal perovskites through controlled chemical etching and confined growth.

infographic.key_insight: Controlled solvent/antisolvent etching creates rectangular cavities inside layered halide perovskite microcrystals for regrowing compositionally distinct, endo-epitaxial heterostructures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a chemical route to designed internal perovskite interfaces without conventional lithography, although solar-cell performance is not demonstrated in the abstract.
method: Etch from the top surface preferentially along crystallographic [100] and [010] directions.
Tune cavities through etching time, temperature, and etchant composition, with interruptible etching cycles.
Regrow distinct layered perovskites inside cavities using sequential precursor addition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports tunable cavity formation, stepwise etching, and confined regrowth across diverse perovskite compositions and antisolvent systems, but provides no quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Reproducible interface quality and compatibility with photovoltaic device fabrication remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures

title: Supercell periodicity biases octahedral tilting and energetics in high-entropy perovskite oxides
authors: Hanzo Tsubota, Wai Kian Tan, Hiroyuki Muto, Atsunori Matsuda, Tom Ichibha, Kenta Hongo
abstract: Odd-period supercells such as $3 \times 3 \times 5$ are often used for equimolar five-component compositions in computational studies of high-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs). However, such cells are known to constrain octahedral tilting because they cannot accommodate all standard tilt patterns (Glazer tilt systems). How strongly this constraint affects HEPOs, whose octahedra respond to local cation environments, remains unclear. Here we show that supercell periodicity systematically biases computed octahedral tilting and energetics. Using a machine-learning interatomic potential, we compared odd-period and tilt-commensurate cells for 13 HEPOs. Odd-period cells yielded smaller and less coherent tilts and higher energies, even after configurational averaging. In ~1,700-atom cells, tilt differences persisted in all compositions and energy differences in most. The bias extended to defects, with lower oxygen vacancy formation energies in odd-period cells for strongly tilted compositions. Based on these findings, a simple design rule for equimolar supercells is proposed to lift this constraint.

infographic.key_insight: Odd-period supercells systematically suppress octahedral tilting and raise computed energies in high-entropy perovskite oxides.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing tilt-compatible supercells can reduce structural and energetic bias in computational screening of perovskite oxides, including oxygen-vacancy predictions.
method: Used a machine-learning interatomic potential to study 13 high-entropy perovskite oxides.
Compared odd-period and tilt-commensurate supercells with configurational averaging.
Evaluated octahedral tilts, energies, and oxygen-vacancy formation energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: In approximately 1,700-atom cells, tilt differences persisted across all 13 compositions and energy differences persisted in most; odd-period cells also lowered vacancy formation energies in strongly tilted compositions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports oxide simulation results, not solar-cell performance, and does not specify the proposed equimolar-supercell design rule.
infographic.paper_title: Supercell periodicity biases octahedral tilting and energetics in high-entropy perovskite oxides

title: Nitrogen Defect Coupling in Epitaxial LaFeO3 From Structural Reconstruction to Water Oxidation
authors: Le Wang, Shan Lin, Min-Ju Choi, Krishna P. Koirala, Mark E. Bowden, Jeffrey A. Dhas
abstract: Earth-abundant ABO3-type perovskite oxides provide a versatile platform for understanding how anion chemistry and defects govern electrocatalytic behavior. Here, we use epitaxial LaFeO3-xNy thin films to reveal how dilute N incorporation (<0.8% N/O) couples to defect formation, structural reconstruction, and water oxidation. Nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed laser deposition introduces N and is accompanied by reduced oxygen content, localized Fe-metal exsolution, and pronounced lattice expansion, while preserving predominantly Fe3+ in the bulk of the film. Ab initio calculations identify a plausible charge-balanced extended defect configuration involving coupled oxygen and Fe vacancies with substitutional N incorporation, reproducing the experimentally observed lattice expansion while preserving the bulk-average Fe oxidation state. The resulting electronic-state redistribution is accompanied by substantially modified electrical transport and nearly two orders of magnitude higher initial oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity than undoped LaFeO3. Under OER conditions, however, the highly active as-grown state is metastable: near-surface N depletion and Fe0 oxidation/removal accompany rapid initial activity decay toward a quasi-steady state. pH-dependent kinetics and post-OER anion redistribution are consistent with possible lattice-oxygen participation. These results establish relationships among dilute anion incorporation, coupled defect reconstruction, electronic properties, and electrochemical behavior in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: Dilute nitrogen incorporation in epitaxial LaFeO3 couples defect formation and lattice expansion to nearly 100-fold higher initial oxygen evolution activity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This water-oxidation study, rather than AI or solar-cell research, suggests anion–defect engineering can enhance earth-abundant perovskite electrocatalysts.
method: Grow epitaxial LaFeO3−xNy films using nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed laser deposition.
Use ab initio calculations to assess coupled nitrogen substitution and oxygen/iron vacancies.
Evaluate electrical transport, OER kinetics, and post-reaction compositional changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: At <0.8% N/O, films show pronounced lattice expansion, predominantly bulk Fe3+, and nearly two orders of magnitude higher initial OER activity than undoped LaFeO3.
infographic.watch_item: The highly active as-grown state is metastable: near-surface nitrogen depletion and metallic iron oxidation/removal accompany rapid initial activity decay.
infographic.paper_title: Nitrogen Defect Coupling in Epitaxial LaFeO3 From Structural Reconstruction to Water Oxidation

title: Electronic-morphological decoupling in mixed-dimensional halide perovskite heterostructures
authors: Mahmoud Samadpour, Alireza Fathi Beiraghvandi, Kazem Meraji, Tristan Sachsenweger Ballantyne, Fuxiang Ji, Mahdi Mohammadi
abstract: Surface morphology is widely considered an indicator of thin-film quality, with smoother films generally expected to exhibit more uniform optoelectronic properties. Here, we demonstrate that substantial surface evolution does not necessarily lead to increased electronic heterogeneity in mixed-dimensional perovskite heterostructures. We investigate how low-dimensional Ruddlesden-Popper capping layers derived from the sterically hindered 5-tert-butyl-phenanthridinium cation affect the spatial distributions of photoluminescence (PL) characteristics and quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) in 3D perovskites. By combining statistical atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis with confocal, spatially resolved PL spectroscopy, we correlate surface topography with microscale optoelectronic properties. Although capping increases surface roughness and height asymmetry, it does not increase electronic inhomogeneity. Instead, the heterostructures exhibit enhanced PL, reduced non-radiative recombination, and improved spatial uniformity of radiative QFLS compared with pristine 3D films. Under accelerated aging, this contrast becomes more pronounced: pristine films develop substantial spatial fluctuations in emission and QFLS, whereas capped heterostructures largely preserve their optoelectronic homogeneity. These findings indicate that the low-dimensional capping layer suppresses aging-induced optoelectronic disorder, demonstrating that electronic uniformity can be maintained despite morphological irregularity. This decoupling provides a design principle for developing durable, high-performance perovskite photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: Low-dimensional capping makes 3D perovskite surfaces rougher while enhancing photoluminescence and preserving electronic uniformity, even under accelerated aging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Surface smoothness alone may be an unreliable quality metric when designing durable perovskite solar-cell interfaces.
method: Form mixed-dimensional heterostructures using 5-tert-butyl-phenanthridinium-derived Ruddlesden–Popper capping layers.
Combine statistical AFM with confocal, spatially resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy.
Compare morphology, emission, and quasi-Fermi level splitting in pristine and capped films under accelerated aging.
infographic.evidence_signal: Despite increased roughness and height asymmetry, capped films showed enhanced emission, reduced non-radiative recombination, and more uniform radiative quasi-Fermi level splitting than pristine films.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report device efficiency, quantitative effect sizes, or aging conditions, limiting assessment of practical photovoltaic gains.
infographic.paper_title: Electronic-morphological decoupling in mixed-dimensional halide perovskite heterostructures

title: Impact of organic spacer cations on the light and thermal stability of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites
authors: Mahesh Eledath-Changarath, Jesús Ortiga-Fibla, Andrés F. Gualdrón-Reyes, Jesús Rodríguez-Romero, Iván Mora-Seró, Ana Cros
abstract: Long-term stability remains a critical challenge limiting the photovoltaic and optoelectronic applications of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites. In these materials, the choice of the organic spacer plays a key role not only in enhancing environmental stability, but also in determining their structural characteristics and carrier dynamics. Here, we present an environmental photo- and thermal-stability analysis of BA2PbI4 and PEA2PbI4 two-dimensional lead halide perovskites by means of confocal micro-Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy techniques. We have investigated two different organic spacers, n-butylammonium (BA) and 2-phenylethylammonium (PEA), which provide comparable room-temperature luminescence in freshly exfoliated perovskite nanoflakes and degrade similarly through the removal of organic components and fast crystal phase decomposition into PbI2 and Pb0. However, we observed that the PEA organic cation significantly improves crystal morphology and suppresses lattice defects, resulting in slower degradation and enhanced resistance to light and thermal stress under ambient conditions. Our findings indicate that structural and chemical engineering, along with surface passivation and encapsulation strategies, are essential for achieving long-term stability in two-dimensional halide perovskite devices. Nevertheless, optimizing the balance between stability and device performance remains a critical consideration.

infographic.key_insight: PEA organic spacers slow degradation and improve ambient light and thermal stability relative to BA spacers in two-dimensional lead iodide perovskites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spacer selection can improve perovskite durability, but long-term device stability also requires defect control, surface passivation and encapsulation.
method: Compared BA2PbI4 and PEA2PbI4 nanoflakes under ambient light and thermal stress.
Probed degradation using confocal micro-Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.
Examined spacer-dependent morphology, lattice defects and decomposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fresh nanoflakes showed comparable room-temperature luminescence, while PEA-based crystals exhibited better morphology, fewer lattice defects and slower degradation despite shared decomposition pathways to PbI2 and metallic Pb.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative stability gains or device-level photovoltaic testing, so improved material durability does not establish longer solar-cell lifetime.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of organic spacer cations on the light and thermal stability of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites

title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites
authors: Ethan Berger, Erik Fransson, Apinya Ngoipala, Lucas Svensson, Priyanka Deswal, Mehmet Baskurt
abstract: Perovskites have been studied for a wide range of applications, from oxide-based ferroelectrics to halide-perovskite photovoltaics. Despite their diverse functionalities, these materials share strong lattice anharmonicity arising from structural instabilities such as polar off-centering and octahedral tilting. These anharmonic distortions strongly influence the low-frequency vibrational response and can be observed in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. However, low-frequency IR and Raman signatures are typically investigated separately, hindering the development of a unified understanding of vibrational spectroscopy across perovskite classes. In this work, we use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate the IR and Raman spectra of oxide perovskites (SrTiO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$), halide perovskites (CsPbBr$_3$, CsSnBr$_3$, and CsGeBr$_3$) and double halide perovskites (Cs$_2$AgAlBr$_6$ and Cs$_2$AgBiBr$_6$). By comparing materials exhibiting polar, tilt-driven and mixed instabilities, we find that polar off-centering leads to enhanced low-frequency IR and dielectric responses, whereas nonpolar modes, particularly octahedral tilting, are associated with Raman central peaks. The strength of the low-frequency features also depends on how strongly the underlying modes couple to polarization or dielectric susceptibility. Finally, we show that the dynamics of these instabilities play an important role, with slow polar reorientations shifting the dielectric response to very low frequencies and overdamped tilting modes producing persistent Raman central peaks. These results establish a unified framework connecting low-frequency IR and Raman spectra to the symmetry, coupling and dynamics of their underlying anharmonic lattice instabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Across perovskites, polar off-centering enhances low-frequency infrared and dielectric responses, while nonpolar octahedral tilting is associated with Raman central peaks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Connecting spectral features to lattice instabilities could help interpret structural dynamics in halide-perovskite solar-cell materials, without directly establishing device-performance gains.
method: Use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate infrared and Raman spectra.
Compare seven oxide, halide and double-halide perovskites.
Relate spectral features to instability symmetry, coupling strength and dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations across seven perovskites link slow polar reorientations to very-low-frequency dielectric response and overdamped tilting to persistent Raman central peaks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative accuracy benchmarks or solar-cell device validation, so predictive reliability and device implications remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites

title: AgBiS2 near-infrared absorbers for thin film tandem photovoltaics
authors: Shiling Dong, Yongjie Wang, Hae-Jun Seok, Mengyuan Huang, Edward Newton, Der Ying Chen
abstract: AgBiS2 has rapidly risen in efficiency as single-junction photovoltaics (PVs), but its potential for tandem PVs is unexplored. Herein, we perform optical modeling based on the experimental absorption spectrum of AgBiS2, revealing that, as the NIR sub-cell, efficiencies exceeding 47.5% are achievable in triple-junction tandems, superseding tandems using Pb/Sn perovskite NIR cells (44.2%). However, fulfilling this potential requires overcoming the limited transport properties of AgBiS2 nanocrystal films, which constrains film thicknesses to only 30-50 nm, severely restricting NIR response. A solution-phase ligand exchange process is herein developed, allowing one-step deposition of passivated AgBiS2 nanocrystals that maintain efficient charge-carrier extraction despite an order of magnitude increase in film thickness. These films enable 24.0%-efficient four-terminal tandems with visible-light-absorbing lead-halide perovskite sub-cells, and monolithic tandems successfully demonstrating voltage addition. AgBiS2 PVs have high stability, retaining >90% of the original efficiency after 3 months of storage in dry air without encapsulation. This work establishes the significant potential of AgBiS2 as a stable and scalable NIR absorber for tandem PVs.

infographic.key_insight: Solution-phase ligand exchange enables thicker AgBiS2 near-infrared absorbers, delivering 24.0%-efficient four-terminal tandems with lead-halide perovskite cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved carrier extraction in thicker AgBiS2 nanocrystal films supports stronger near-infrared harvesting for stable, scalable thin-film tandem photovoltaics.
method: Model tandem performance using the experimental AgBiS2 absorption spectrum.
Use solution-phase ligand exchange for one-step deposition of passivated, thicker nanocrystal films.
Integrate AgBiS2 with visible-light-absorbing perovskite cells in four-terminal and monolithic tandems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 24.0% four-terminal tandem efficiency, voltage addition in monolithic tandems, and >90% efficiency retention for AgBiS2 cells after three months in dry air without encapsulation.
infographic.watch_item: The >47.5% triple-junction efficiency is a modeled potential, not a demonstrated device result; storage stability also does not establish operational durability.
infographic.paper_title: AgBiS2 near-infrared absorbers for thin film tandem photovoltaics
